lead: A biosensor must pick one molecule out of a blood sample full of others, and the bio-recognition element does that picking. Enzymes catalyse one substrate, antibodies bind one antigen, nucleic acid probes pair with one complementary sequence. The element's kinetics or binding constant sets the sensor's range and detection limit. Glucometer strips, pregnancy tests and DNA test cards in Indian labs all rest on this layer. This chapter covers the three families, the numbers that describe them, and how they are fixed to a transducer.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the component chain.

blocks.text: An enzyme is a protein catalyst. It binds one substrate at its active site, converts it, and is released unchanged, so one molecule cycles many times. Activity is quoted in international units: 1 U = 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute. Glucose oxidase, used on every glucose strip, oxidises β-D-glucose and is nearly blind to other sugars.

blocks.where: v is the rate (µmol min⁻¹ per mg of enzyme); Vmax is the rate when every site is occupied; S is substrate concentration; Km is the substrate concentration giving v = Vmax/2.

blocks.text: Km measures how tightly the enzyme holds its substrate: small Km means tight binding and early saturation. At S = 19·Km, v = 0.95·Vmax. Above that, doubling S barely changes v, so the sensor cannot resolve two high concentrations; the useful range ends well below 19·Km. On an electrode the enzyme is immobilised, substrate must diffuse through the layer, and the apparent Km usually rises.
An unfavourable equilibrium is pulled forward by removing product continuously. An enzyme electrode does exactly this by oxidising the product at the electrode surface.

sections.h3: Antibodies and nucleic acids: binding sets selectivity

blocks.text: An antibody is not a catalyst. It binds an antigen and stays bound; it is neither consumed nor turned over. Affinity is described by the dissociation constant Kd = [antibody][antigen]/[complex]; smaller Kd means tighter binding. A whole IgG has two sites, so multivalent avidity can be far stronger than one site's Kd suggests. Detection is label-free when binding itself changes mass or charge on the transducer, and labelled when a fluorescent or enzyme tag reports the event.

A nucleic acid probe is a short single strand, for example a 20-base oligomer. It finds its target by Watson–Crick pairing: A with T, G with C. Hybridisation strengthens as G+C content rises (three hydrogen bonds per G–C pair against two for A–T) and as salt concentration rises, which shields the negative phosphate backbones; it weakens as temperature rises. The melting temperature Tm is where half the duplexes have separated. Cells and chemoreception serve as recognition layers in whole-cell sensors.

Immobilisation methods: adsorption is simple but leaks; covalent coupling is stable; gel entrapment holds whole cells and enzymes; self-assembled monolayers of thiols on gold give an ordered, reproducible surface.

figure.caption: Three recognition families and the reading that fixes each sensor's range: Km for the enzyme, Kd for the antibody, Tm and salt for the nucleic acid probe.

spec.aria: A tree with the bio-recognition layer at the root branching into enzyme, antibody and nucleic acid, each labelled with the constant that decides that sensor's measuring range.

examples.question: A glucose-oxidase electrode has Vmax = 120 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ and Km = 5.0 mmol/L. (a) Find v at S = 2.0 mmol/L. (b) Show that S = 5.0 mmol/L gives half of Vmax. (c) Find the concentration giving 95% of Vmax. (d) On the immobilised strip the apparent Km is 12 mmol/L; state the new half-saturation level.
steps: At S = 2.0 mmol/L: numerator 120 × 2.0 = 240; denominator 5.0 + 2.0 = 7.0; v = 240/7.0 = 34.3 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹.
At S = 5.0 mmol/L: v = 120 × 5.0/10.0 = 60.0 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, exactly Vmax/2, which is the definition of Km.
On the surface the half-saturation point moves to the apparent Km = 12 mmol/L, so the same enzyme saturates later.
examples.answer: (a) 34.3 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, (b) 60.0 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ = Vmax/2, (c) 95 mmol/L, (d) 12 mmol/L.
examples.check:
Vmax = 120.0
Km = 5.0
S1 = 2.0
v1 = Vmax*S1/(Km+S1)
print(round(v1,1))
v2 = Vmax*Km/(Km+Km)
print(round(v2,1))
print(round(19*Km,1))
print(12.0)

traps: An antibody is not a catalyst: it binds without turnover, so Vmax and Km do not apply to it.
Km is a concentration in mmol/L, not a rate; the rate units belong to Vmax.
Smaller Kd means tighter binding; a large Kd is the weak antibody.
The Km measured in free solution is not the apparent Km of the immobilised layer.

quiz.a: 1 U = 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute.

quiz.q: Why does an antibody not obey Michaelis–Menten kinetics?
quiz.a: It binds without turnover; there is no catalytic cycle, so Vmax and Km do not apply.

quiz.q: Vmax = 80 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, Km = 4.0 mmol/L. Find v at S = 12 mmol/L.
An immobilised enzyme shows apparent Km of 20 mmol/L against 5 mmol/L in solution. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Substrate must diffuse through the layer; crowding and wrong orientation reduce accessible active sites.

quiz.q: Which is tighter binding, Kd = 1 nM or Kd = 10 µM?
A 20-mer probe has high G+C. What happens to Tm and to stringency?
quiz.a: Tm rises; hybridisation is stronger, so the wash must be hotter or lower in salt to keep specificity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses lateral-flow antibody tests, aptamers as synthetic recognition elements, CRISPR-based nucleic acid tests and molecularly imprinted polymers. Surface crowding and Debye-length screening decide whether a label-free antibody sensor works in undiluted serum. Search 'aptamer biosensor', 'lateral flow immunoassay' and 'Debye length screening' next.
